title: The chemistry of cooking
text: A recipe is, at bottom, an experiment with edible results, and food science has begun to read it that way. Melt butter gently and little happens; heat it further and it browns, generating hundreds of new compounds and the flavour we rather inadequately describe as {{1}} (NUT). This browning is the Maillard reaction, and for generations cooking was treated as an art beyond {{2}} (ANALYSE). That era has ended. Food laboratories can now explain why steaks benefit from resting, why chillies burn, and why bread needs a little salt to {{3}} (DEEP) the flavour of the crumb. Some findings are immediately practical: chilling potatoes before roasting alters their starch and produces a noticeably crisper crust, an effect any home cook can verify {{4}} (PERSON). Other findings upset tradition. Cooks long insisted that searing meat seals in the juices; careful measurement has shown the claim to be {{5}} (TRUE), though resting meat really does keep it juicier, which explains the {{6}} (WIDE) accepted advice to wait before carving. Best of all, understanding seems to sharpen rather than spoil the pleasure: a souffle may obey physics, but at table it remains an act of {{7}} (GENEROUS). Kitchen and laboratory, far from rivals, make natural {{8}} (ALLY).

gaps.explanation: 'an art beyond analysis' — the noun of this family is analysis.
'needs salt to deepen the flavour' — verb from deep.
'shown the claim to be untrue' — negative prefix un-.
'the widely accepted advice' — adverb from wide.
'an act of generosity' — noun from generous.
